concepts.heading: Bodily Autonomy as a Human Right
concepts.alt: A guide standing tall with a hand on her heart inside a glowing outline of herself
concepts.plain: Your body is yours. You have the right to decide what happens to it.

concepts.heading: What Bodily Autonomy Means
concepts.alt: A guide holding a key and a compass
concepts.plain: You decide about touch, medical care, sex and having children.

concepts.heading: Bodily Autonomy in Your Relationships
concepts.alt: Three guides standing together, each holding their own key
concepts.plain: Partners can make agreements, but no one gets to control another person's body.

concepts.heading: Intersections with Identity
concepts.plain: Not everyone gets this right equally. Some groups face extra barriers.

checks.prompt: Bodily autonomy is described as a…
checks.explanation: Foundational human right. Bodily autonomy — the right to make decisions about your own body without external coercion — is a foundational human right that underpins all other rights.

options: Deciding what happens to your own body
checks.explanation: Deciding what happens to your own body. Bodily autonomy is the principle that every person has the right to decide what happens to their own body.

fe6c4411-4946-4e3b-8cd3-ce9f4f8cae52.takeaway: Your body is yours, and decisions about it belong to you.

concepts.heading: Contraception & Informed Choice
concepts.plain: To choose birth control well you need full, honest information.

concepts.heading: The Contraception Landscape
concepts.alt: A guide holding a tray of different small boxes and a calendar
concepts.plain: There are many methods, each with pros and cons.

concepts.heading: Informed Choice Means Real Choice
concepts.alt: A guide choosing between several open doors, a lightbulb above her
concepts.plain: A real choice means knowing your options, with no one pressuring you.

concepts.heading: Contraception in Different Relationships
concepts.plain: Your birth control plan should fit your relationships, and change when they do.

concepts.heading: Healthcare Advocacy
concepts.alt: He raises a hand with a checklist while talking to her, a doctor in a white coat
concepts.plain: You may need to speak up to get respectful care. You are allowed to.

checks.prompt: Making informed choices about contraception requires…
checks.explanation: Comprehensive, unbiased information. Making informed choices about contraception requires access to comprehensive, unbiased information — something that many people never receive due to inadequate sex education, cultural taboos, and healthcare systems that don't prioritize…

checks.prompt: Are all healthcare providers knowledgeable and affirming about every relationship style?
options: No, so you may need to speak up for yourself
checks.explanation: No, so you may need to speak up for yourself. Not all healthcare providers are knowledgeable about or affirming toward ENM, LGBTQ+, or polyamorous patients.

47e2a583-1ee2-401f-9f75-3123715a5141.takeaway: A real choice about birth control needs full information and no pressure.

concepts.heading: Reproductive Justice vs. Reproductive Rights
concepts.plain: "Rights" and "justice" are two different ideas here.

concepts.heading: Reproductive Rights: A Limited Framework
concepts.alt: A guide holding a single document with a balance-scale icon
concepts.plain: Reproductive rights is mostly about what the law allows.

concepts.heading: Reproductive Justice: A Comprehensive Framework
concepts.alt: Three guides holding a large ring together that links small icons of a home, a heart, a child and a health cross
concepts.plain: Reproductive justice asks whether people can really use those choices in their lives.

concepts.heading: Who This Affects Most
concepts.plain: Unfair rules hit hardest for people whose families or identities don't fit the usual mold.

concepts.heading: Historical Context
concepts.plain: The history includes people being stopped from having children against their will.

concepts.heading: Taking Action
concepts.alt: A guide rolling up her sleeves, a megaphone in one hand and a book in the other
concepts.plain: The lesson lists ways to act: learn more, support groups and speak up.

checks.prompt: The traditional reproductive rights frame focuses mainly on…
options: Legal access to abortion and contraception
checks.explanation: Legal access to abortion and contraception. The reproductive rights movement, as traditionally framed, focuses primarily on legal access to abortion and contraception.

checks.prompt: Who created the reproductive justice framework in 1994?
checks.explanation: Twelve Black women. The reproductive justice framework was created in 1994 by 12 Black women who recognized that the reproductive rights movement didn't address their lived reality.

9205f0dd-79d2-4873-9a3a-5172e8b46ea3.takeaway: Having a legal right is not the same as being able to use it in real life.

concepts.heading: Access, Equity & Reproductive Advocacy
concepts.plain: A right only helps if people can actually reach the care.

concepts.heading: The Access Gap
concepts.alt: A guide standing at the edge of a wide gap, a far-off clinic sign with a medical cross on the other side
concepts.plain: Distance, cost and insurance keep many people from getting care.

concepts.heading: The Digital Divide
concepts.alt: A guide holding a phone with a padlock on its screen, looking careful
concepts.plain: Data from apps and phones can reveal private health details.

concepts.heading: What You Can Do
concepts.alt: A guide holding a jar of hearts and wearing a volunteer badge
concepts.plain: The lesson lists ways to help, like giving money or time.

concepts.heading: Advocacy in Your Relationships
concepts.plain: Start close to home by talking openly with partners and friends.

concepts.heading: Community-Level Action
concepts.alt: Four guides forming a human chain, passing boxes marked with hearts
concepts.plain: Local groups help people with money, rides and a place to stay.

concepts.heading: Systemic Advocacy
concepts.plain: You can also contact lawmakers and back groups led by the people most affected.

concepts.heading: Intersectional Solidarity
concepts.plain: This links to other fairness issues, like money, race and disability.

checks.explanation: Equitable access. Reproductive freedom means nothing without equitable access. Systemic barriers disproportionately affect marginalized communities, creating a landscape where your zip code, race, income, and identity determine your reproductive options.

checks.prompt: Which kind of app does the lesson flag as a privacy concern?
checks.explanation: Period tracking apps. The lesson lists period tracking apps sharing data as a privacy concern.

25180ad7-bd2d-46d0-8e47-b4c9d2d099b8.takeaway: Access to care is uneven, and there are concrete ways to help close the gap.
